correctness.rationale: The Gram kernel is exactly 1-max(t,s)^(1/alpha). Differentiation produces the stated Sturm–Liouville equation with u(1)=0 and vanishing weighted flux at 0; solving by Bessel branches excludes the J_{+nu} branch and makes the positive J_{-nu} zeros the entire simple spectrum. Classical Bessel zero asymptotics give the \(1/n\) law. The trace identities follow independently from direct kernel integrals. The small-power boundary uses a normalized Bessel power-series convergence, uniform root lower bounds, dominated convergence and the classical Rayleigh sum to obtain both the nonleading root limits and the -3/4 top correction. The large-power boundary is continuity of positive roots. The independent 350-point finite-matrix tests check normalization for seven exponents and boundary profiles; they are not infinite proofs.

value.rationale: Domanov’s power-substitution Volterra operator is natural and has a known contrasting geometric ordinary spectrum, so exact approximation numbers and operator ideals are motivated invariants. The complete Bessel spectrum supplies all finite-rank approximation errors, the sharp Schatten threshold, and moments, while two genuinely different Bessel boundary regimes reveal quantitative rank-one concentration and opposing scaling at large powers. These facts are not generic normalization checks or arbitrary parameter slices.
